section.p: Absolute convergence gave us a safer kind of infinite sum. If
Conditional convergence is different. It survives because positive and negative terms balance each other. That balance is real, but it is fragile.
The next question is simple to ask:
section.md: \text{Can we rearrange the terms of an infinite sum?}
section.p: For finite sums, the answer is yes. For infinite sums, the answer depends on what kind of convergence we have.

subsection.title: Finite sums can be rearranged freely
subsection.p: A finite sum does not care about order:
Both sides use exactly the same four numbers. Addition is commutative and associative, so rearranging finitely many terms does not change the answer.
This is one of the habits we bring from algebra.
But an infinite sum is not completed all at once. It is a limit of partial sums:
So the order matters because the order controls the path taken by the partial sums.
A finite sum has a last term. An infinite sum does not.
subsection.md: \text{Infinite addition is not just finite addition with more terms.}

exercise.title: Why can order matter for an infinite sum but not a finite one?

statement.p: Finite addition is commutative: rearranging finitely many terms cannot change the answer. In your own words, why is an infinite sum not just finite addition with more terms, and why does order control the path taken by the partial sums?

hint.p: A finite sum has a last term, so the whole collection is added at once. An infinite sum is a limit of running totals, and a different order is a different sequence of running totals.

exercise.title: How can the same terms produce a different sum?

statement.p: A rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series can converge to \frac32 of the original sum. In your own words, why does using the same terms in a different order change the accumulated limit, and what does that warn about conditional convergence?

hint.p: Putting two positive terms before each negative term changes how the running totals climb and drop. The terms are the same; the path of partial sums is not.

subsection.p: For a conditionally convergent series, the positive terms and negative terms each have infinite total size.

A rearrangement can disturb that balance.

subsection.title: The Riemann rearrangement idea
subsection.p: The last observation leads to a striking theorem.

statement.p: If a series converges conditionally, then its terms can be rearranged to converge to any real number chosen in advance.

subsection.p: A full proof belongs in a later analysis course, but the idea is accessible.
Suppose the target number is T.
Start adding positive terms until the partial sum rises above T. This is always possible because the positive terms have infinite total sum.
Then add negative terms until the partial sum falls below T. This is always possible because the negative terms have infinite total size.
Then add positive terms again until the partial sum rises above T. Then negative terms until it falls below T. Continue forever.
The overshoots get smaller because the individual terms of any convergent series must approach 0. So the rearranged partial sums are forced closer and closer to T.

subsection.p: This theorem is one of the clearest signs that infinity changes the rules. A finite sum cannot be rearranged to become a different number. A conditionally convergent infinite sum can.

exercise.title: Why can a conditionally convergent series be steered to any target?

statement.p: The Riemann rearrangement theorem says that the terms of a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any chosen real number. In your own words, why does infinite positive supply and infinite negative supply make that possible, and why do the overshoots still shrink?

hint.p: You can always add enough unused positive terms to rise above the target, then enough unused negative terms to fall below it. Individual terms of a convergent series go to zero, so the overshoots become small.

subsection.title: Why absolute convergence is safer
subsection.p: Absolute convergence prevents this danger.

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: Given an error tolerance \varepsilon>0, choose N so large that the absolute tail is small:
Now take any rearrangement of the series. Go far enough in the rearranged partial sums so that all of the first N original terms
After that point, the only possible difference between the rearranged partial sum and the full sum S comes from terms in the tail
The total absolute size of that tail is less than \varepsilon. Therefore the rearranged partial sums must stay within \varepsilon of S.
Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, the rearranged series converges to S.
This is why absolute convergence is stronger than ordinary convergence. It says the series has finite total size, not merely a lucky cancellation pattern.
The next section collects the main traps in this chapter. Each trap comes from using a test after forgetting one of its hypotheses.

exercise.title: Why does absolute convergence make order irrelevant?

statement.p: If \sum |a_k| converges, every rearrangement converges to the same sum. In your own words, why does a small absolute tail lock the sum in place no matter which later terms appear next?

hint.p: Once the first N original terms have all appeared, any remaining difference comes from the tail. Finite total size makes that tail smaller than any chosen tolerance, independently of order.
